passage: In the small-town school near Kottayam, the boys from the upper village and the lower village had been fighting all term over the football ground. Joseph, the PE teacher, tried a fix: put both groups in the same detention room after school. The upper-village boys were made monitors because their marks were better. Joseph watched through the window. Nobody talked. The monitors wrote the lower-village boys' names on the board for "noise." One lower-village boy muttered, "See? They always think they're bosses." By Friday the fights were worse. Joseph sat with the headmistress, Gurleen ma'am. "I made it worse," he said. "Same room, no reason to cooperate, and I handed one side power." She nodded. "Then give them a reason." They planned a single inter-school football team: mixed, captain chosen by vote, the district cup as the goal.

qa.q: Why were the upper-village boys made monitors?
qa.a: They were made monitors because their marks were better.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said "I made it worse"?
qa.a: Joseph felt regretful and troubled, realising his plan had hardened the rivalry instead of easing it.

qa.q: Why is a single mixed football team with a voted captain a better plan?
qa.a: It gives both groups a common goal, equal status and the school's support, which are the conditions under which contact reduces prejudice.

qa.q: How might the lower-village boys have seen the detention room?
qa.a: They likely felt humiliated and controlled, which confirmed their belief that the upper-village boys always act like bosses.

grounding: A teacher sees that bringing rival groups together with unequal status and no shared aim only hardens stereotypes, and plans equal, goal-based teamwork instead.

passage: After a fight between students who supported rival Lisbon football clubs, the school tried a "unity lunch." Ines, the form teacher, watched it from the canteen doorway. The two groups were placed at the same long table with no plan, no task, and the kids from the club with the bigger stadium were handed the serving spoons. Within ten minutes, jokes turned into chants. Jana, a quiet fifteen-year-old from the smaller club's side, put down her fork and left. Ines followed her into the corridor. "They made us wait for them to serve us," Jana said, blinking fast. "Like we're guests in their house." Ines didn't argue. She went back and thought about what had happened. Sitting together had only proved each side's stories. What they needed was a problem neither could solve alone, like the school film project, with equal roles and the head's support.

qa.q: What did the kids from the club with the bigger stadium get handed?
qa.a: They were handed the serving spoons.

qa.q: What was Ines thinking as she went back to the canteen?
qa.a: Ines felt troubled and reflective, realising the lunch had only confirmed each side's stories because it lacked a shared aim and equality.

qa.q: What could make the next mixing attempt work?
qa.a: A shared project like the school film, with equal roles and the head's backing, would give the groups a real reason to depend on each other.

qa.q: How did Jana experience the unity lunch?
qa.a: Jana felt humiliated and unwelcome, like a guest waiting to be served in someone else's house.

grounding: A teacher notices that bringing rival groups together without a shared goal and with unequal roles hardens stereotypes, and considers equal, goal-based contact.

passage: Anjali, you're nervous about working with the girls from the other school? Let me tell you about our play. I'm Vinita, and when I was fifteen, our convent in Varanasi joined the municipal girls' school across the river for the annual drama festival. Everyone in my class said they were rough and loud. They said the same about us: snobs. The teacher gave us one play, Savitri, and split every role between the schools. I was Savitri; a girl called Munni was Yama, the god of death. I couldn't act my big scene without her lines. So we practised on the ghats every evening. She taught me to project my voice; I helped her with the English script. On the night, when the lights went down, I didn't think "municipal girl." I thought, Munni's got my back. Forty years later, she still calls on my birthday.

qa.q: Which role did Munni play?
qa.a: Munni was Yama, the god of death.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling about the other school's girls before the play?
qa.a: Vinita felt wary, having heard her class call them rough and loud, much like they called Vinita's class snobs.

qa.q: Why was splitting every role between the schools a key choice in the story?
qa.a: It made the girls depend on each other to succeed, so shared effort turned them into one team instead of rivals.

qa.q: How might Munni have felt practising on the ghats with Vinita?
qa.a: Munni may have felt respected and valued as an equal, teaching voice while receiving help with the English script.

grounding: An elder recalls how teenagers from different schools who had to depend on each other in a play turned "them" into "us".

passage: The robot had to be ready by nine a.m. for the inter-school science fair, and at eight p.m. the power went out across half of Amritsar. Sahil, sixteen, from the officers' colony, and Amandeep, from the old city lanes, sat in Amandeep's courtyard with a battery lantern. A month ago they'd barely spoken; Sahil's friends called the old-city boys "tapori," and Amandeep's cousins called the colony boys "show-offs." The teacher had paired them anyway. Now Sahil knew the code and Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop. Neither could finish without the other. At midnight the motor sparked and died. Sahil groaned. Amandeep calmly re-soldered the joint. At two a.m. the robot rolled forward. Sahil punched the air. "We did it!" Neither of them noticed he'd said "we." The next day at the fair, their friends from both sides crowded round to watch.

qa.q: What did Amandeep know from his uncle's electrical shop?
qa.a: Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop.

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling when he punched the air?
qa.a: Sahil felt thrilled and triumphant, sharing the success with Amandeep as a real teammate.

qa.q: What made this pairing work better than a talk about tolerance?
qa.a: Each boy had a skill the other needed for a shared goal, so they had to depend on each other, which built trust.

qa.q: How might their friends from both sides see the pair at the fair?
qa.a: Their friends might start to see the other side differently, watching the two work as a proud team.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods on a science team depend on each other to succeed, and shared effort turns "them" into "us".

passage: In the school auditorium in Dadar, Jatin, fifteen, from the chawl across the railway line, was cast as the villain. Chinmay, from the glass tower near the sea, was the hero. For the first rehearsals they stood at opposite ends of the stage and barely looked at each other. Chinmay's friends whispered about the chawl boys' "language"; Jatin's friends joked about tower boys who'd never taken a local train. But the big fight scene needed trust: Jatin had to catch Chinmay mid-fall. The first three times Chinmay flinched and they collapsed. Jatin said, "Just trust me, yaar." The fourth time, Chinmay let go. Jatin caught him. They practised it forty more times over two weeks. On opening night, the audience gasped. Backstage afterwards, Chinmay bought vada pav for the whole cast and handed Jatin the first one.

qa.q: How many more times did they practise the fall?
qa.a: They practised it forty more times over two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling the first three times he flinched?

qa.q: What helped the two boys become a team?
qa.a: The fight scene forced them to rely on each other, and repeated practice built trust that talks couldn't.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Chinmay handed him the first vada pav?
qa.a: Jatin probably felt respected and included, seeing the rivalry replaced by friendship.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods in a school play must depend on each other, and shared effort turns rivals into a team.

subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]
passage:

Third week: In a team meeting, the manager asked her to explain "Northeast culture" to everyone. She did, stiffly, feeling like a brochure. That night she called her sister and said she was tired of speaking for eight states.
Second month: Sahil asked her to join his quiz team for the office fest. Not because she was Manipuri, but because he'd heard her answer a film question. They practised together, argued about cricket, and won. Afterwards he asked what music she liked. She told him. For once, she felt like Madhuri, not an example.

qa.a: The manager asked her to explain "Northeast culture" to everyone.

qa.a: Sahil moved from curious outsider questions to seeing her as a teammate with her own tastes, like her music.

grounding: A young adult who is the only one from her region at work feels curious eyes and pressure to represent everyone, until good contact lets her be an individual.

I'm your Anirban uncle, your mother's old friend, and at nineteen I was the only Bengali in an engineering hostel in Patiala. I felt like I had to represent all of Bengal, and I was failing. I stayed in my room a lot that first term. Then my roommate Harpreet asked me to join the college football team. subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]
passage: The group presentation was due in two days, the Delhi hostel's Wi-Fi had crashed, and Nirmala, twenty, was the only Adivasi student in her sociology batch. When the professor assigned topics, a classmate had turned to her. "You can do the tribal section, na? You'd know." Nirmala had spent the week feeling eyes on her in the canteen, as if everything she did would stand for her whole community. Now, huddled in the common room around one phone hotspot, Mridul, her group partner, looked at the plan. "Actually, what do you want to present? You said you liked urban housing." Nirmala blinked. "I do." "Then take housing. I'll do the other bit and ask you if I get stuck." She felt her shoulders drop. For the first time that term she felt like herself, not a sample.

passage: Neelam, you're taking over the new warehouse team? Let me tell you what I did at the garment factory in Tiruppur. I'm Yamini; I was twenty-five, the only woman supervisor on the floor. Half the tailors were Tamil, half had come from Bihar and Odisha. They ate separately, took breaks separately, called each other names I won't repeat. My manager said, "Just keep them apart." Instead I made mixed lines: every line needed a cutter, a stitcher and a checker, one from each side. The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's. The first week was ugly. A man mocked a Bihari worker's Tamil. I stopped the line and said, "Nobody laughs at anyone here. Next time, you go home." It didn't happen again. By Diwali, I saw them sharing tiffins. I never gave one speech.

qa.q: Who set the target for the Diwali order?
qa.a: The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she stopped the line?
qa.a: Yamini felt firm and angry at the mockery, determined not to let anyone be laughed at.

qa.q: Why was ignoring the manager's advice to keep the groups apart a key decision?
qa.a: Mixing lines with equal roles and a shared target gave the workers a real reason to depend on each other, which softened attitudes.

qa.q: How might the Bihari worker have felt when Yamini stopped the line?
qa.a: He likely felt protected and respected, seeing that the supervisor would not tolerate mockery of him.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a young supervisor, forming mixed work lines with equal roles and a common goal, refusing mockery, and seeing attitudes soften.

passage: Rain had flooded the relief warehouse in Kochi, and Payal, twenty-five, had forty volunteers from two colleges that famously disliked each other. On the first day, the St. Thomas students sorted and the Govt. College students were sent to carry sacks. By noon, there were sneers about "labour" and "posh kids." Payal stopped everything. She rebuilt the plan: mixed teams of four, two from each college, each team fully responsible for one relief camp's kits, packing and delivery. Roles would rotate every shift. When Nazia, from St. Thomas, laughed at someone's accent, Payal took her aside. "Not here. Not once." Nazia nodded, red-faced. By the third day, teams were competing to finish their camp first. Payal saw Nazia and a Govt. College boy soaked to the knees, lifting a crate together, laughing.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she stopped everything at noon?
qa.a: Payal felt alarmed and determined, seeing the unequal roles breed sneers between the colleges.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Mixed teams with shared responsibility for a camp and rotating roles gave everyone equal status and a common goal, so rivalry turned into teamwork.

qa.a: Nazia felt embarrassed, going red, but seemed to accept the boundary, and later joined in the shared work.

grounding: A young team lead rebuilds relief work into mixed teams with equal roles and a common goal, refuses mockery, and sees attitudes soften through shared work.
